title: Root: dicere, dictum (to say)
core: All three descend from Latin *dicere* (to say), and all three name speech that comes down from a position of authority rather than across from an equal. None of them is conversation: one party pronounces, the other receives. What separates them is *which part of the act* each word names — the imposing, the finished pronouncement, or the accusation.

words.nuance: The only one naming the **act of imposing**, and the only verb — it takes an object (terms, a schedule, the peace) and a victim who had no say. Its distinguishing test is the absence of negotiation: **dictate** is what you do *instead of* consulting. It also has a cool impersonal use the others lack entirely — *the budget dictates the timeline* — where no authority figure exists and it means only "determines, leaves no choice."

Names the **finished utterance itself**, not the act — a quotable, portable line you can attribute. Unlike a **dictate**, it compels nobody; its force is the speaker's standing, not power over you. That attributability also separates it from *proverb* or *adage*: a **dictum** has a named author behind it, and in law (*obiter dicta*) it is authoritative in tone yet explicitly not binding.

The only accusatory member, and the only one that takes **of** — an **indictment** is always *of* something, aimed at a target. Where a **dictum** pronounces a truth and a **dictate** imposes a rule, an **indictment** charges guilt: it presents evidence, not opinion, which is why *damning*, *searing*, and *stinging* cling to it. It opens a case rather than settling one — accusation, never verdict.

exam_note: The GRE usually wants the figurative **indictment** ("the results are an indictment of the policy" = damning proof, not a grand jury) and the impersonal **dictate** ("supply dictates price" = determines), while test-takers hunt for a courtroom or a tyrant.
